guides.title: TOPIK: the Test of Proficiency in Korean
guides.text: Test dates, registration and past papers. Many universities, employers and some visa types ask for a TOPIK level.

guides.title: Understanding visa types
guides.text: Your visa type (체류자격) decides what you may do in Korea: study, work, or live with family.
tips: D-2 is for university students and D-4 for language trainees.
E-9 is for workers through the Employment Permit System (EPS).
E-7 is for specific professional jobs.
F-6 is for marriage migrants.
Each visa allows certain activities only. Check what yours allows on Hi Korea or by calling 1345.

guides.title: Registering for your residence card
guides.text: If you will stay in Korea for more than 90 days, you must register as a foreign resident within 90 days of entering Korea and receive a residence card.
tips: Book an appointment at your local immigration office through Hi Korea.
Bring your passport, a photo, the application form and documents for your visa type.
Carry your residence card with you.
Report a change of address within the legal deadline. Check Hi Korea for the current rule.

guides.title: Extending or changing your stay
guides.text: Apply before your permitted stay ends. Late applications and working outside your visa's permitted activities can lead to fines or other penalties.
tips: Check your expiry date on your residence card now and set a reminder.
Many applications can be made online or by appointment on Hi Korea.
For your own situation, ask the Immigration Contact Center (1345) or a qualified professional. DHL can't give legal advice.

guides.text: Visas, residence cards, appointments and e-applications. Immigration Contact Center: 1345 (multilingual).

guides.title: Know your rights at work
guides.text: Korean labor law protects foreign workers too.
tips: Ask for a written employment contract, in a language you understand, and keep a copy.
The minimum wage applies to foreign workers.
Keep your own record of working hours and pay.
For labor questions, call the Ministry of Employment and Labor counseling center at 1350.
A DHL mentor can listen and help you find the right office.

guides.title: Korean workplace basics
guides.text: Simple habits that help you build trust at work.
tips: Arrive a little early; punctuality matters.
Greet colleagues when you arrive and leave.
Use polite speech (존댓말) with supervisors and older coworkers.
Ask when you don't understand: 다시 한 번 말씀해 주세요 (please say it again).

guides.title: Preparing a Korean résumé
guides.text: Korean applications usually have two parts: a résumé (이력서) and a self-introduction letter (자기소개서).
tips: Many Korean résumés include a professional photo.
List your visa type and Korean level (such as your TOPIK level) clearly.
In the self-introduction letter, explain why you want this job and how you will contribute.
Ask a Korean friend or DHL mentor to check your Korean before you apply.

guides.title: Talk to a mentor about your career
guides.text: Planning your next step in Korea or back home? A mentor can listen and help you think it through.

guides.title: Study in Korea
guides.text: Official information for international students, including admissions and scholarships.

guides.title: Campus life basics
guides.text: What to expect at a Korean university.
tips: Visit your university's international student office early. They help with visas, housing and registration.
Seniors (선배) and juniors (후배) matter in Korean student culture. Seniors often help newcomers.
Group projects (팀플) are common. Communicate often and share work fairly.
Student visa holders usually need permission before working part-time. Ask your international office first.

guides.title: Student communities at DHL
guides.text: Meet other international students for Bible study, fellowship and friendship.

guides.title: Getting around
guides.text: Korea's public transport is fast, cheap and easy once you know the basics.
tips: Buy a T-money card at a convenience store or subway station, and top it up with cash.
Naver Map and KakaoMap give better directions in Korea than most international map apps.
Tap your card when you get on and off buses so transfers are discounted.

guides.title: Understanding Korean housing
guides.text: What to check before you sign a contract or pay a deposit.
tips: Know the difference between 월세 (monthly rent with a deposit) and 전세 (a large lump-sum deposit).
Check that the landlord owns the property before paying a deposit.
Get a written contract and ask a Korean-speaking friend or a DHL mentor to read it with you.
Report your new address when you move.

guides.title: Opening a bank account
guides.text: Bring your passport and residence card. Banks may also ask for a document from your employer or school, and some limit new accounts at first. Ask at the branch what you need.

guides.title: Healthcare in Korea
guides.text: Many foreign residents who stay six months or more are enrolled in National Health Insurance. Check your status on the NHIS site.
tips: For everyday illness, visit a local clinic (의원). For serious conditions, go to a hospital (병원).
Bring your residence card to every visit.
Pharmacies (약국) fill prescriptions and sell basic medicine.
In an emergency, call 119.

guides.title: Trash and recycling
guides.text: Household trash goes in volume-based trash bags (종량제 봉투) sold at convenience stores. Food waste and recyclables are separated. Rules differ by district, so ask your neighbors or building manager.
